title: Disappearing stories
brief: People post photos and short clips that vanish after 24 hours. Followers tap through a tray of stories every day, and the poster sees who looked. Deleting on time matters: storage must not grow forever.

clarify.a: The story must stop being visible and the files should be deleted soon after to save money.
Only the poster. Every view tap is an event that has to be recorded, though it can arrive a few seconds late.

clarify.q: Is a story a hot item?
clarify.a: Sometimes. A celebrity story can be viewed by millions in an hour. Most stories are seen by a few friends.

clarify.q: Do stories have to be kept for anyone later?
clarify.a: No. They disappear for everyone, which makes the storage story easy: nothing is kept forever.

notes: Each story is about 3 MB in total (approx.).
Stories are deleted after 24 hours. Storage depends on how well you expire them.

hints: What makes this storage cheaper than a photo app? Think about what happens to a story after one day.
Object storage can delete files by age on its own. A short retention keeps the storage bill flat instead of growing every day.
Try: phones -> CDN -> app servers -> key-value store for the tray and view lists, object storage with a 1-day retention for the files. View events go through a queue.

editorial.summary: A story app stores a lot of media but only keeps it for one day, so the cheapest design is the one that deletes on time. Let object storage expire files by itself, serve the media through a CDN, keep the tray of stories in a fast key-value store, and push "seen" events through a queue.

designs.name: One-day storage, CDN, event queue
designs.why: The retention setting deletes old stories without any code. The CDN keeps today's hot stories at the edge. The tray and the seen list are tiny records in a key-value store, and view events flow through a queue so a celebrity story does not overwhelm the database.

tradeoffs: A retention rule makes storage flat, but it also makes deletion permanent. A "save my story" feature needs a separate copy.
A one-hour CDN cache keeps the bandwidth bill low, but a story deleted early can stay visible for a while. Short caches cost more and are safer.
View events can arrive late, so the "seen by" list may be a few seconds behind. Nobody notices.
A cold archive makes no sense here. The whole point is that stories disappear.
editorial.realWorld: Stories apps are among the heaviest media-upload workloads: hundreds of millions of stories a day across the largest apps (approx.). Because everything expires after a day, storage grows with the daily upload rate and not with the age of the service.
